title: Volume and surface area of {{term:prism}}s and {{term:cylinder}}s
summary: Turn prisms and cylinders, find the {{term:base-solid}}, fill them layer by layer to see why volume = base area × height, and open the {{term:net}} to work out the {{term:lateral-area}} and the {{term:total-surface-area}}.
guide: This studio follows KS3 "volume of cuboids and other prisms, including cylinders" (Iran G7 ch.6, Afghan G8 ch.6). All lengths are in cm, and the cylinder missions take π as 3.14.

Turn the solid by dragging it, with the arrow buttons or with the arrow keys. "Hidden edges" shows the edges at the back as dashed lines. The line under the picture says which faces can be seen from where you are.
The base is the cross-section the prism is made of when you slice it parallel to the ends; it does not have to be at the bottom. A prism lying on its side still has its two triangles as its bases.

Common slips: taking a rectangle as the base, counting only the faces you can see, writing πr²h for a cylinder's curved surface, mixing up cm² and cm³, and adding the edges instead of finding the volume. Each one gets its own feedback.

engine.instruction-pick: Turn the solid and tap faces.
engine.label-prism: Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face
engine.label-keys: Use the arrow keys to turn it.

find-bases.title: Where is the base?
find-bases.prompt: This small wooden ramp is a {{term:prism}} lying on one of its faces. Predict first: which faces are its {{term:base-solid}}s? Then turn it and tap both bases.
find-bases.hint: A prism's bases are two identical faces opposite each other. All the other faces are rectangles. One base is hidden at the back, so turn the solid.
find-bases.success: Well done! The two triangles at the ends are the bases of this prism: identical and opposite each other.
find-bases.why: The ramp is lying on a rectangle. Why is that rectangle not the base of the prism?
find-bases.model: The base does not depend on which face the solid stands on. If you slice the prism parallel to its base, every slice is exactly the same triangle. Slices parallel to that rectangle are not all the same size. So the bases are the two triangles, and this is a triangular prism.

feedback.pick-empty: You haven't chosen a face yet. Tap the faces on the picture, or choose them from the list below it.
feedback.wrong-base: You chose a rectangle. The ramp is lying on a rectangle, but the bases are the two identical faces opposite each other. Which two faces match?
feedback.one-base: You found one base! A prism has two. Turn it to see the triangle at the other end.

fill-wedge.title: Fill it layer by layer
fill-wedge.prompt: Fill the same ramp with triangular layers 1 cm thick. Predict: how many layers will fit? When it is full, write its {{term:volume}} with the right unit.
fill-wedge.hint: Each layer is a triangle with the two shorter sides 3 and 4, so its area is {{frac:1/2}} × 3 × 4. The prism is 6 long: how many layers is that?
fill-wedge.success: Well done! Each layer is 6 cm³ and there are 6 layers: volume = 6 × 6 = 36 cm³.
fill-wedge.why: Why is the volume of a prism "area of the base × height"? Explain with the layers.
fill-wedge.model: Each 1 cm layer is a triangle the size of the base, so its volume in cm³ is the base area: 6 cm³. The prism is 6 cm long, which is 6 layers. So volume = base area × height = 6 × 6 = 36. Here the "height" of the prism is the distance between the two bases, even when the prism is lying down.

feedback.layers-empty: There are no layers yet. Press +.
feedback.layers-few: It isn't full yet. Add layers until you reach the other end.
feedback.no-unit: The number is right! Now choose the unit.
feedback.area-for-volume: The number is right, but cm² measures area. Volume counts little cubes: cm³.
feedback.length-unit: cm measures length. Volume is measured in cm³.
feedback.one-layer: That is just one layer. How many layers does the prism have?
feedback.wrong-base: You worked out 3 × 4 × 6, so you took the rectangle it lies on as the base (or left out the {{frac:1/2}} in the triangle's area). That is a whole box, and the ramp is half of it.
feedback.surface-for-volume: 84 is the area of all the faces: how much paint would cover it. Volume is how much space is inside: count the layers.
feedback.edges-sum: You added the lengths of the edges. That is a length, not a volume. Multiply the area of one layer by the number of layers.
feedback.three-sides: You multiplied 3, 4 and 5. 5 is the sloping side of the triangle. Find the base area from the two shorter sides, then multiply by the length.
feedback.too-big: Your number is bigger than the volume. Area of one layer × number of layers.
feedback.too-small: Your number is smaller than the volume. Area of one layer × number of layers.

box-net.title: Open the box
box-net.prompt: We want to cover a 5 × 3 × 4 box in wrapping paper. Predict: how many faces does it have? Then unfold the box and write its {{term:total-surface-area}}.
box-net.hint: The closed box only shows three faces. Unfold it: every face has a matching face the same size.
box-net.success: Well done! 6 faces in 3 pairs: 2 × (15 + 20 + 12) = 94 cm².
box-net.why: Why can't you find the total surface area from just the faces you can see in the picture?
box-net.model: From any direction you can see at most 3 faces of a box, but it has 6. The back, left and bottom faces are hidden. Each hidden face is the same size as the face opposite it, so the total is twice the three faces you see: 2 × 47 = 94.

feedback.no-unit: The number is right! Choose the unit too.
feedback.volume-for-area: The number is right, but cm³ measures volume. Wrapping paper covers a surface: cm².
feedback.length-unit: cm measures length. Write the area in cm².
feedback.visible-only: You only counted the three faces you can see. Turn or unfold the box: the back, left and bottom faces need paper too.
feedback.lateral-only: That is the {{term:lateral-area}}: just the four faces round the sides. You forgot the top and the bottom.
feedback.one-base: You left out one of the two bases. The box has a top and a bottom.
feedback.volume-for-surface: 60 is the volume of the box (5 × 3 × 4): how much fits inside. We want the area of the outside.
feedback.edges-sum: You added the edges. Wrapping paper covers the faces: add the areas of the faces.
feedback.too-big: Your number is bigger than the total surface area. Unfold the box and add the areas of the 6 faces.
feedback.too-small: Your number is smaller than the total surface area. Unfold the box and add the areas of the 6 faces.

can-label.title: The label on a can
can-label.prompt: A can of beans is a {{term:cylinder}} with {{term:radius}} 5 cm and height 10 cm. How many cm² is the paper label round it? Predict what shape the label is when you take it off, then unfold the can. (π = 3.14)
can-label.hint: The label opens into a rectangle. Its height is the height of the can, and its length is the distance round the circle: 2 × π × 5.
can-label.success: Well done! The label is a rectangle 31.4 long and 10 high: 2πr × h = 31.4 × 10 = 314 cm².
can-label.why: Why is the length of the label's rectangle the same as the circumference of the base?
can-label.model: The label goes exactly once round the can and its two ends meet. So when you open it out, its bottom edge is the distance round the circle: 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4. That is why the curved surface area of a cylinder is 2πr × h.

feedback.empty: Write the area of the label.
feedback.no-unit: The number is right! Choose the unit too.
feedback.volume-for-area: The number is right, but the label is a surface: cm², not cm³.
feedback.length-unit: cm measures length. Write the area in cm².
feedback.volume-for-surface: You worked out πr²h: that is the volume of the can, how many beans fit inside. The label is a rectangle 2πr long and h high.
feedback.total-for-lateral: You added the circles at the top and bottom too. The label only goes round the side, not over the lids.
feedback.half-around: You worked out π × r × h, which is only half way round the can. The circumference is 2πr.
feedback.diameter-for-radius: You used the diameter (10) as the radius (5). The circumference is 2 × π × radius.
feedback.pi-value: You took π as 3. In this mission π = 3.14.
feedback.too-big: Your number is bigger than the area of the label. Unfold the can: length × height of the rectangle.
feedback.too-small: Your number is smaller than the area of the label. Unfold the can: length × height of the rectangle.

can-volume.title: How much does the can hold?
can-volume.prompt: Now fill the same can with circular layers 1 cm thick. How many {{term:cubic-centimetre}}s of beans fit inside? (π = 3.14)
can-volume.hint: Each layer is a circle of radius 5: π × 5 × 5. The can is 10 cm high, so there are 10 layers.
can-volume.success: Well done! The base is 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 cm², and there are 10 layers: 78.5 × 10 = 785 cm³.
can-volume.why: The label was 314 cm² and the volume is 785 cm³. Why can't you compare these two numbers?
can-volume.model: Area says how many 1 × 1 squares cover a surface; volume says how many 1 × 1 × 1 cubes fit inside. One is a surface and the other is a space, so their units are different. The volume of a cylinder works like a prism: base area × height = πr² × h.

feedback.layers-empty: There are no layers yet. Press +.
feedback.layers-few: The can isn't full yet. Add layers until you reach the top.
feedback.no-unit: The number is right! Choose the unit too.
feedback.area-for-volume: The number is right, but volume is written in cm³, not cm².
feedback.length-unit: cm measures length. Volume is measured in cm³.
feedback.one-layer: 78.5 is just one layer: the area of the base. The can has 10 layers.
feedback.label-for-volume: 314 was the area of the label. The label covers the outside; volume is how much fits inside.
feedback.surface-for-volume: That is the total surface area of the can (the label and both lids). Work out the volume with the layers.
feedback.edges-sum: You added the circumferences of the two circles. Volume = base area × height.
feedback.diameter-for-radius: You used the diameter (10) as the radius (5). The area of a circle is π × radius × radius.
feedback.pi-value: You took π as 3. In this mission π = 3.14.
feedback.too-big: Your number is bigger than the volume. Area of one layer × number of layers.
feedback.too-small: Your number is smaller than the volume. Area of one layer × number of layers.
